title: Columban (23 November)
hook: an Irish monk who founded monasteries across Europe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cecilia, the Roman martyr musicians call their own. Your line was she sang in her heart.

A small boat pushes off from the Irish coast. In it sits a monk named Columban with a few companions. Nobody is chasing them. No bishop has sent them away. They are leaving on purpose, and they are not planning a return trip. The monk who later wrote Columban's life, Jonas of Bobbio, tells how he crossed the sea and walked into the kingdoms of the Franks, a stranger in a country where he knew no one. He found wild, half-empty hills and started building. He made his home out of being away from home.
screen: `A BOAT LEAVES IRELAND.` → `NO ONE SENT THEM.` → `A STRANGER BUILDS IN THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: Columban's leaving had an old pattern behind it. In Genesis, God's call to Abram is a hard one. In the Douay-Rheims: "Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred." No map. Just go. The letter to the Hebrews looks back on Abraham and the others who lived in tents and says they confessed that they were "pilgrims and strangers on the earth." Some Irish monks took that line personally. They spoke of a pilgrimage for Christ: leaving your own people, not for a holiday and not for a shrine, but as an offering, with the road itself as the prayer. Columban lived it. In the hills of Gaul he founded monasteries, Annegray and then Luxeuil, and people came to join him. He wrote a rule for his monks, strict and short. He also made enemies. Jonas tells how a king's household asked him to bless the king's sons, born outside the king's marriage, and Columban refused. The quarrel ended with him ordered out of the kingdom. So he kept walking. He crossed the Alps into Italy, and at Bobbio he founded one more monastery, and there his road ended. A tourist goes for the view and comes home. A pilgrim of this kind lets the unfamiliar place strip things away: the habits, the reputation, the comfortable chair. Columban never kept a comfortable chair for long.
screen: `GO FORTH OUT OF THY COUNTRY.` · `PILGRIMS AND STRANGERS ON THE EARTH.` · `LUXEUIL, THEN EXILE, THEN BOBBIO.` · `A PILGRIM LETS THE ROAD CHANGE HIM.`

segments.voice: Get up and go somewhere you don't usually sit, a different chair, the back step, the far corner of the room, and notice that the place feels a little strange; let that strangeness wake you up. If you pray, offer this new spot to God, the way Abram was told to go to a land he would be shown; if you don't, notice what you can see from here that you never see from your usual seat.
Columban. The Irish monk who left home on purpose, planted monasteries from Gaul to Italy, and treated being a stranger as his way of following Christ.
Your line: pilgrim for christ. For Columban, the road itself was the prayer. Day one thousand forty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Saint Columban is remembered on 23 November, with particular devotion in Ireland and at the places his monasteries stood, such as Luxeuil in France and Bobbio in Italy.

notes: Audit (fresh pass): Douay-Rheims Genesis 12:1 and Hebrews 11:13 checked; Jonas's account (Annegray, Luxeuil, refusal to bless the king's sons, expulsion, Bobbio) fairly summarized. No change.
Confirm Challoner wording of Genesis 12:1 ('Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred') and Hebrews 11:13 ('pilgrims and strangers on the earth').

From Jonas's Life: departure from Ireland with companions (count left out on purpose), Annegray and Luxeuil, the refusal to bless Theuderic's sons (presented by Brunhild), expulsion, Bobbio. Confirm the summary; the king and queen are left unnamed.
'Irish monks spoke of a pilgrimage for Christ' (peregrinatio pro Christo): confirm phrasing; stated generally, not as a claim about all Irish monks.
'He wrote a rule for his monks, strict and short': confirm the description of the Regula monachorum.

Editor pass: 'Irish monks took that line personally' softened to 'some Irish monks'; the stock 'here's what makes a pilgrim different' passage tightened and the interpretive 'he seems to have liked it that way' cut.
